chunks: Ibn Mahbub from Abu Ayyub from Samaan said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a Muslim who killed a dhimmi (non-Muslim subject). He said: 'This is a severe matter that people cannot bear. He should give their family the blood money of a Muslim, until he is deterred from killing the people of the land (non-Muslims generally) and from killing the dhimmi.' Then he said: 'If a Muslim became angry at a dhimmi and wanted to kill him and take his land, and paid their family eight hundred dirhams, then killing among the dhimmis would increase.' And whoever kills a dhimmi unjustly, it is forbidden for the Muslim to kill a dhimmi as a retribution (qisas), as long as they paid the jizya and did not deny it. As for the specific narration of Abu Basir, we have narrated from him that their blood money is eight hundred, like the other reports. And what his report contained regarding the distinction between the Jews, Christians, and Magians, he also narrated that there is no distinction between them and that they are equal in blood money. And we have presented that from him and from others, which adds to the clarification.

key_terms.أَبُو بَصِيرٍ: Abu Basir: A prominent narrator of hadith
key_terms.أَهْلُ السَّوَاد: Ahl al-Sawad: The people of the land (non-Muslims)
key_terms.جِزْيَة: Jizya: Poll tax levied on non-Muslim subjects
key_terms.دِيَة: Diyah: Blood money or compensation for killing
key_terms.ذِمِّي: Dhimmi: A non-Muslim subject living under Islamic rule

ai.seo_question: What is the blood money (diyah) for a Muslim who kills a non-Muslim dhimmi according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) establishes that unjustly killing a dhimmi incurs the blood money of a Muslim (diyat al-mu'min) rather than the standard dhimmi rate, a severe penalty designed to prevent the proliferation of killings against protected non-Muslims. This ruling highlights the principle of 'deterrence through severity' (li-yankula), ensuring that the lower financial cost does not incentivize murder. The text further contextualizes this within Shia jurisprudence by reconciling apparent contradictions in narrations regarding whether blood money distinctions exist among Jews, Christians, and Magians, ultimately affirming their equality in this specific legal aspect.
